summary: RFCs 6513, 6514 and others describe how a service provider offers Multicast VPN service to its customers, using point-to-multipoint or multipoint-to-multipoint trees in the backbone. This proposed standard describes the use of ingress replication tunnels as one type of such tree.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC explains how a service provider can carry a customer's multicast across its backbone by simply sending a separate copy of every packet down a unicast path to each receiver, and how the routers agree on which copies belong together.

questions: what is ingress replication in mvpn
how is an ir p-tunnel identified
what is a pmsi tunnel attribute
subtitle: How multicast VPN routers join, leave and label ingress replication tunnels, where the parent sends one unicast copy per child.

tldr.problem: The Multicast VPN specifications describe provider tunnels that carry customer multicast across a service provider's backbone, but they never say how a router joins one of the simplest of those tunnels, the one where the parent sends a separate unicast copy of every packet to each child.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC makes the procedures explicit: the tunnel is identified by the route that advertises it rather than by the Tunnel Identifier field, a router joins it by originating a Leaf A-D route, and the MPLS label it assigns has to follow rules that let the far end detect packets from the wrong source.
tldr.outcome: The result is that an implementation can build and maintain ingress replication tunnels using the existing MVPN route types, with no new protocol elements. RFC 7988 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 6513 and RFC 6514, and it was later updated by RFC 10018.

facts.label: PTA fields
facts.value: Tunnel Type, MPLS Label, Tunnel Identifier, Flags

today: RFC 7988 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 6513 and RFC 6514, and it was itself updated by RFC 10018. It has not been obsoleted, so its identification and label rules are the ones an MVPN implementation should follow.

sections.title: What an Ingress Replication P-Tunnel Is
sections.content:
RFC 6513, RFC 6514 and other RFCs describe procedures by which a Service Provider may offer Multicast VPN (MVPN) service to its customers. Those procedures create point-to-multipoint (P2MP) or multipoint-to-multipoint (MP2MP) tunnels, called P-tunnels, across the provider's backbone, and customer multicast traffic is carried through them.

One of the supported P-tunnel technologies is known as "ingress replication" or "unicast replication", and this document uses the acronym "IR" for it. With the single exception of IR, the P-tunnel technologies supported by the MVPN specifications are preexisting IP multicast or MPLS multicast technologies. Each of those has its own set of specifications, its own setup and maintenance protocols, its own syntax for identifying specific multicast trees, and its own procedures for adding or removing a router from a tree. IR P-tunnels have no prior specification for setting up and maintaining the P2MP trees; the procedures and protocol elements are specified in the MVPN specifications themselves, and all the signalling and setup is done using the BGP Auto-Discovery (A-D) routes defined in RFC 6514. The unicast tunnels used to carry the data may of course have their own setup protocols, such as RFC 5036 or RFC 3209.

Earlier RFCs sometimes describe an IR P-tunnel as "consisting of" a set of unicast tunnels, and this document argues that the description is not quite accurate. It obscures the fact that an IR P-tunnel is really a P2MP tree whose nodes must maintain multicast state in both the control and data planes, and it obscures the fact that the unicast tunnels used by a particular IR P-tunnel need not be specific to that P-tunnel: a single unicast tunnel can carry the multicast traffic of many different IR P-tunnels, and can also carry unicast traffic.

Some of the MVPN specifications ask a PE router to join the P-tunnel identified in a particular route, but until now there has been no explicit specification of how to identify an IR P-tunnel, how to join one, or how to prune from one. This document fills those gaps. It also discusses the MPLS label allocation policies needed for correct operation with an IR P-tunnel, and the timer policies needed when switching a customer multicast flow from one IR P-tunnel to another. It provides no new protocol elements and no fundamentally new procedures; its purpose is to make explicit how to use the protocol elements and procedures of RFC 6513 and RFC 6514. In the event of any conflict, this document takes precedence, and it updates both RFCs.
sections.plainLanguage: Most provider tunnels are built with a purpose-made multicast protocol. This one needs none: the provider's own multicast routing already exists, and the tree is held together by the same BGP routes that announce customer VPNs.

sections.title: How Data Travels Along an IR P-Tunnel
sections.content:
An IR P-tunnel is a P2MP tree whose nodes are BGP speakers that support the MVPN procedures of RFC 6514. In general the nodes are Provider Edge (PE) routers, Autonomous System Border Routers (ASBRs), or, if RFC 7524 is supported, Area Border Routers (ABRs). Provider tunnels may be "segmented" or "non-segmented". A non-segmented IR P-tunnel is a two-level P2MP tree consisting only of a root node and a set of nodes that are children of the root; in an MVPN context the root is an ingress PE and the children are egress PEs.

As with any P2MP tree, each node holds multicast state for the tunnel: it knows the identity of its parent node and the identities of its child nodes. The MVPN specifications call the parent node the "Upstream Multicast Hop", or UMH, and that node may be a PE, an ASBR or an ABR.

What distinguishes an IR P-tunnel from any other P2MP tree is how a packet gets from a parent to a child. The parent labels the packet with a label that the child has assigned to that P-tunnel, places the packet in a unicast encapsulation and unicasts it to the child through a unicast tunnel. That unicast tunnel need not be specially created for this P-tunnel: it can be any P2P or MP2P unicast tunnel that will get the packets to the child, and a single such tunnel may be carrying packets of several different P2MP trees as well as unicast traffic. The parent repeats this for each child, making one copy per child, and does not use Layer 2 multicast, IP multicast or MPLS multicast to reach its children. As a result, multiple copies of a packet may be sent out of a single interface.

Because data along an IR P-tunnel is always unicast from parent to child, it is convenient to think of the tunnel as a P2MP tree whose arcs are unicast tunnels. But the unicast tunnels need not be specific to any one IR P-tunnel: if R1 is the parent of R2 on two different IR P-tunnels, a single unicast tunnel from R1 to R2 may carry data for both. All that is required is that when the packets arrive at R2, R2 sees the P-tunnel label at the top of the label stack, and its further processing depends on that label. Typically the unicast tunnels are the LSPs that already exist to carry unicast traffic, either MP2P LSPs created by LDP or P2P LSPs created by RSVP-TE, but any kind of unicast tunnel may be used, and a unicast tunnel may have any number of intermediate routers that keep no multicast state for the IR P-tunnel and are not even aware that it exists.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router on the tree makes its own copy of every packet and sends each copy down an ordinary unicast path to one child. The path may be shared with other traffic, so the receiver relies on a label to work out which tree a packet belongs to.

sections.title: How an IR P-Tunnel Is Identified
sections.content:
There are four MVPN BGP route types in which P-tunnels can be identified: Intra-AS I-PMSI A-D routes, Inter-AS I-PMSI A-D routes, S-PMSI A-D routes and Leaf A-D routes. Whenever a route identifies a P-tunnel, a PMSI (Provider Multicast Service Interface) Tunnel attribute is added to it. That attribute has four fields: Tunnel Type, MPLS Label, Tunnel Identifier and Flags. RFC 6514 defines only one bit in the Flags field, the Leaf Information Required bit.

Most P-tunnel types are set up and maintained by a specific protocol, and that protocol has its own way of naming the trees it builds: mLDP uses an FEC element, and PIM-SSM uses the (S,G) pair. In those cases the Tunnel Identifier field of the attribute carries a tree identifier defined by the setup protocol.

IR P-tunnels are entirely set up and maintained by BGP A-D routes and are not associated with any other setup protocol, so the way of naming them is very different. When an IR P-tunnel is identified in an S-PMSI, Intra-AS I-PMSI or Inter-AS I-PMSI A-D route, its identifier is defined to be the NLRI of that route, including the Route Type and Length fields. The identifier of the IR P-tunnel therefore does not appear in the Tunnel Identifier field of the attribute at all; it appears in the NLRI field of the A-D routes used to advertise and set up the tunnel. An advertising A-D route is considered to identify an IR P-tunnel only if it carries an attribute whose Tunnel Type field is set to "IR", which is the value 6.

When the IR P-tunnel is identified in an S-PMSI A-D route or in an Inter-AS I-PMSI A-D route, the Leaf Information Required bit of the Flags field MUST be set. In that case the Tunnel Identifier field has no significance whatsoever and MUST be ignored on reception, though its length MUST still be the length of an IP address in the service provider's backbone address space. If the bit is not set, the Tunnel Identifier field does have significance, but it does not identify the IR P-tunnel.

When an IR P-tunnel is identified in a Leaf A-D route, its identifier is the Route Key field of the route's NLRI, and the Tunnel Identifier field again has significance without identifying the tunnel. Because the identifier is the NLRI, two different advertising A-D routes cannot advertise the same IR P-tunnel: in the terminology of RFC 6513, an IR P-tunnel can instantiate only a single PMSI.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnel is named by the route that announces it, not by a number inside the route. That is the fix: previously the field that was supposed to name the tunnel had no defined meaning for this kind of tunnel, so nothing said which tunnel a router was joining.

sections.title: Joining an IR P-Tunnel
sections.content:
The procedures for joining an IR P-tunnel depend on whether it has been advertised and, if so, on how. Joining an unadvertised IR P-tunnel is only possible when using the "global table multicast" procedures of RFC 7524.

For an advertised IR P-tunnel, the procedure depends on whether the advertising route has the Leaf Information Required bit set. When it is set, the router joining the tunnel must first determine its UMH for that P-tunnel. If the advertising route contains a P2MP Segmented Next Hop Extended Community, the UMH comes from that community; otherwise it comes from the route's next hop. The router then originates a Leaf A-D route whose NLRI contains the IR P-tunnel identifier as its route key, and it MUST identify the UMH by attaching an IP-address-specific Route Target to that route, with the address of the UMH in the Global Administrator field. The Leaf A-D route must also carry a PMSI Tunnel attribute whose Tunnel Type is "IR", whose Tunnel Identifier is set as described in Section 5, and whose MPLS Label field is a non-zero value. That label is the P-tunnel label, and it has to satisfy the constraints of Section 7.

When the Leaf Information Required bit is not set, which can only happen for an IR P-tunnel advertised in an Intra-AS I-PMSI A-D route, the picture is simpler. If an IR P-tunnel is advertised in the Intra-AS I-PMSI A-D routes originated by the PE routers of a given MVPN, the Intra-AS I-PMSI can be thought of as being instantiated by a set of IR P-tunnels: each PE is the root of one such tunnel and the other PEs are children of the root. A PE joins all these tunnels at once by originating an Intra-AS I-PMSI A-D route whose attribute has Tunnel Type "IR", a Tunnel Identifier as described in Section 5, and a non-zero MPLS Label. That label is what the child node uses to associate a received packet with the I-PMSI of a particular MVPN, so the label allocation policy must ensure that the binding from label to I-PMSI is one to one.

Pruning works in the opposite direction. A router that joined a tunnel by originating a Leaf A-D route can leave it by withdrawing that route, for example because it no longer needs any of the flows travelling over the P-tunnel. A router that joined via the Intra-AS I-PMSI route prunes itself by withdrawing that route, which is not usually done unless the router is removing itself entirely from a particular MVPN. A router that needs to stay joined but reach the tunnel through a different parent changes the Route Target of its Leaf A-D route so that it identifies the new parent. The parent node must notice when a child prunes itself, because that affects its own multicast state: the pruning may look like an explicit withdrawal of the Leaf A-D route, or like a change in the Route Target of one, and the effect on the parent's state is the same in both cases.
sections.plainLanguage: To join a tree, a router sends out a route that says which tree it wants and which router it should receive from. To leave, it withdraws that route, or points it at a different parent.

sections.title: The Tunnel Identifier Field of the Attribute
sections.content:
When the Tunnel Type field of a PMSI Tunnel attribute is set to "IR", the Tunnel Identifier field does not contain the IR P-tunnel identifier, and this section says what it does contain. The field is significant only under one of two conditions: the attribute is carried by a Leaf A-D route, or the Leaf Information Required bit of the Flags field is not set.

When one of those conditions holds, the Tunnel Identifier field must contain a routable IP address of the originator of the route. That address is used by the UMH to determine the unicast tunnel it will use to send data along the IR P-tunnel identified by the route key, to the originator of the Leaf A-D route. How the unicast tunnel is determined from the address, and how the tunnel is set up and maintained, are both outside the scope of this document. Section 4 of RFC 6515 must be applied when the attribute is carried in a Leaf A-D route, because it describes how to tell whether the field carries an IPv4 or an IPv6 address.

If neither condition holds, the Tunnel Identifier field is of no significance and MUST be ignored on reception.
sections.plainLanguage: The leftover field in the route is not used to name the tunnel. When it is used at all, it holds the address of the router that sent the route, so that the upstream router knows where to send the data.

sections.title: MPLS Labels and Duplicate Packets
sections.content:
The MPLS Label field of the attribute is not always significant either. It is significant only when the attribute is carried in a Leaf A-D route, or when the Leaf Information Required flag is not set. Because that flag is always set for an S-PMSI or Inter-AS I-PMSI A-D route, the label is never significant in those route types. Where it is significant, the label is the P-tunnel label that the originator of the route assigns to the IR P-tunnels identified by the route's NLRI. Where it is not significant it SHOULD be set to zero on transmission and MUST be ignored on reception.

Section 6 explains why the label matters. RFC 6513 has a procedure called "Discarding Packets from the Wrong PE", which requires an egress PE to work out which PE a multicast packet came from. The assumption here is that an egress PE infers the ingress PE by examining the packet's P-tunnel label. That works exactly the same whether the unicast tunnels are IP tunnels or MPLS LSPs. Looking at the source address of the encapsulating IP header instead would be undesirable: with segmented P-tunnels that address might not be the ingress PE's, it is not guaranteed to be the address the ingress PE uses for the MVPN signalling, and for extranet functionality it is the packet's ingress VRF that must be inferred, which the IP source address cannot give.

That leaves one case where the label cannot carry the information: when the egress PE joined the IR P-tunnel using the Intra-AS I-PMSI procedure. There the ingress PE and the UMH are the same, and no label can be assigned uniquely to a particular ingress PE or UMH. In that case, duplicate prevention on the IR P-tunnel requires either Single Forwarder Selection or native PIM procedures.

The label allocation rules follow from this. The RFC defines the "root of an IR P-tunnel": the router named in the Originating Router's IP Address field for an S-PMSI or Intra-AS I-PMSI NLRI, the router named in the Ingress PE's IP Address field for the global table multicast form, and, for an Inter-AS I-PMSI NLRI, the combination of a Route Distinguisher and an AS. If an egress PE originates two Leaf A-D routes with different route keys whose IR P-tunnels have different roots, it MUST NOT specify the same MPLS label in both, because the same label must not be assigned to two IR P-tunnels with different roots.

With segmented tunnels that rule is necessary but not sufficient, because an egress node may change its parent node on a given tunnel by changing the Route Target of its Leaf A-D route, and for a period the old and the new parent may both send data for the same flow. So whenever the egress node changes the Route Target it attaches to a Leaf A-D route, it MUST also change the MPLS Label in that route's attribute, which lets it tell packets from the old parent apart from packets from the new one. At any given time a router MUST consider itself to have only a single parent node on a given P-tunnel and MUST discard traffic that arrives on that P-tunnel from a different parent.

Where extranet functionality is not implemented, a PE may instead assign a label that is unique for the ordered triple of root, parent node and egress VRF. To support the extranet procedure "Do Not Deliver Packets from the Wrong P-tunnel", the labels must instead be unique for the ordered triple of root, root RD and parent node. Intermediate nodes have their own rules: two Leaf A-D routes they originate may share a label only if their parent node is the same, their forwarding state sends either tunnel's packets to the exact same set of downstream neighbours, and the same encapsulation is applied to both. An intermediate node may always specify distinct non-zero labels instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The label on the packet is what tells the far end where the traffic came from, and the rules make sure that one label never stands for two different trees. If a router moves to a new parent, it must change the label too, so that it can throw away the old parent's copies.

sections.title: Timers When Changing Parent
sections.content:
When a child node decides to change its UMH for a P-tunnel, it modifies the Route Target of its Leaf A-D route so that it identifies the new parent rather than the old one, and it modifies the attribute to change the MPLS Label. The NLRI is not modified; only the Route Target and the attribute change.

It is desirable for such a switch of UMH to use a "make before break" technique, so that the old UMH does not stop sending packets of the given P-tunnel to the child until the new UMH has started sending them. The problem is that the control-plane operation does not permit the child to first join through the new UMH and later prune itself from the old one: a single control-plane operation has both effects. So the old UMH MUST continue transmitting to the child node for a period of time after it sees the child's Leaf A-D route being withdrawn, or its Route Target changing to identify a different UMH. This timer, the "parent-continues" timer, SHOULD have a default value of 60 seconds and SHOULD be configurable.

Because the child advertised a different label for the IR P-tunnel to the new UMH than it advertised to the old one, it can tell the packets transmitted by the new UMH apart from those transmitted by the old UMH. At any given time the child accepts packets of that P-tunnel from only one parent and discards those from the other. To get the make-before-break behaviour, the child needs to continue accepting packets from the old UMH for a period of time, after which it discards them and accepts only those from the new UMH. Once the child modifies the Route Target it MUST run a timer, the "switch-parents-delay" timer, which SHOULD default to 30 seconds and SHOULD be configurable. The child MUST continue to accept packets of the given P-tunnel from the old UMH until the timer expires, although once it receives a packet of that P-tunnel from the new UMH it MAY consider the timer to have expired. The "parent-continues" timer MUST be longer than the "switch-parents-delay" timer, and both are specific to a given IR P-tunnel.
sections.plainLanguage: Moving to a new parent is one step, not two, so there is a window where both parents could be sending the same traffic. Two timers manage that: the old parent keeps sending for a while, and the new router keeps accepting the old copies for a shorter while.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC has one sentence here. No security considerations are raised by this document beyond those already discussed in RFC 6513 and RFC 6514.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is said here. The security rules of the two MVPN documents it updates still apply.
